title: How does a rolling update work (`maxSurge`/`maxUnavailable`), and how do you roll back quickly (`kubectl rollout undo`) — and why might a rollback not restore the previous state (ConfigMap/Secret/DB changes persist across revisions)?
shortTitle: Rolling Updates, Fast Rollback, and Why Rollback May Not Fully Restore State

s1_definition.profdef: A rolling update is Kubernetes' default Deployment strategy that replaces old Pods with new ones gradually, governed by `maxSurge` (how many extra Pods above the desired count may be created) and `maxUnavailable` (how many Pods may be missing during the update). `kubectl rollout undo` reverts the Deployment to a previous ReplicaSet revision. A rollback only restores the Pod template (image, env, resources); it does NOT revert external state such as a ConfigMap, a Secret, or a database schema that changed alongside the deployment.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India is replacing all the teller software on 10 counters. A rolling update means you upgrade one or two counters at a time while the rest keep serving customers, so Rajesh and Priya are never turned away. If the new software is buggy, `rollout undo` is like telling every counter "go back to yesterday's version." But if yesterday's upgrade also rewrote the shared ledger format in the vault, rolling back the counter software does NOT un-rewrite the ledger — that permanent change outlives the rollback.
s1_definition.oneliner: Rolling updates swap Pods gradually with `maxSurge`/`maxUnavailable`, `rollout undo` reverts the Pod template fast, but it never undoes ConfigMaps, Secrets, or database migrations.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A rolling update is Kubernetes' default Deployment strategy that replaces old Pods with new ones gradually, governed by `maxSurge` (how many extra Pods above the desired count may be created) and `maxUnavailable` (how many Pods may be missing during the update). `kubectl rollout undo` reverts the Deployment to a previous ReplicaSet revision. A rollback only restores the Pod template (image, env, resources); it does NOT revert external state such as a ConfigMap, a Secret, or a database schema that changed alongside the deployment.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India is replacing all the teller software on 10 counters. A rolling update means you upgrade one or two counters at a time while the rest keep serving customers, so Rajesh and Priya are never turned away. If the new software is buggy, `rollout undo` is like telling every counter "go back to yesterday's version." But if yesterday's upgrade also rewrote the shared ledger format in the vault, rolling back the counter software does NOT un-rewrite the ledger — that permanent change outlives the rollback.

**One line to remember:** Rolling updates swap Pods gradually with `maxSurge`/`maxUnavailable`, `rollout undo` reverts the Pod template fast, but it never undoes ConfigMaps, Secrets, or database migrations.

sections.s2_technical:
When you change a Deployment's Pod template (for example a new image tag), Kubernetes creates a new ReplicaSet and scales it up while scaling the old ReplicaSet down. `maxSurge` controls how many Pods may exist above the desired replica count during the transition — a value of 25% on 4 replicas allows 1 extra Pod. `maxUnavailable` controls how many of the desired Pods may be unavailable at once — 25% on 4 replicas means at least 3 must stay serving. Setting `maxUnavailable: 0` with `maxSurge: 1` gives a zero-downtime, one-at-a-time ramp, which is what I use for a banking payment service.

Readiness probes are essential here: Kubernetes only counts a new Pod as available once its readiness probe passes, so a broken new version that never becomes ready will stall the rollout instead of taking down the service. You can bound this with `progressDeadlineSeconds`, after which the Deployment is marked failed.

Kubernetes keeps a history of ReplicaSet revisions, limited by `revisionHistoryLimit`. `kubectl rollout history deployment/transfer-service` lists them, and `kubectl rollout undo deployment/transfer-service --to-revision=5` reverts to a specific one. Under the hood this simply scales the chosen old ReplicaSet back up and the current one down — another rolling operation, so rollback is also gradual and respects the same surge and unavailability rules.

The crucial senior point is what rollback does NOT cover. A Deployment revision snapshots only the Pod template. If version 6 of your service shipped alongside a new ConfigMap value, a new Secret, or a forward database migration, then `rollout undo` restores the old container image but leaves the ConfigMap, Secret, and database schema at their new values. If the old image cannot read the new schema, rollback makes things worse, not better. This is why database migrations in banking must be backward compatible — expand then contract — so that both the old and new code can run against the same schema during and after a rollout. For config, I avoid mutating a ConfigMap in place; instead I create a new immutable ConfigMap per release and reference it from the Pod template, so that a template rollback automatically points back at the old config too.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India we deploy the Transfer Service many times a day. Two real problems shaped how we do rolling updates and rollbacks.

Problem 1 — we must never have an outage during an upgrade, because at any second Rajesh could be sending money to Priya. If we replaced all Pods at once and the new version was broken, every transfer in flight would fail. This is exactly what a rolling update with `maxUnavailable: 0` and `maxSurge: 1` solves — we add one new Pod, wait for it to pass readiness, then retire one old Pod, so capacity never drops below the desired level.

Problem 2 — one release shipped a bad fee-calculation change AND a database migration that added a NOT NULL column. When we ran `rollout undo`, the old image came back but the database still had the new NOT NULL column, and the old code did not populate it, so inserts failed. This taught us why rollback does not restore external state and why migrations must be backward compatible.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `RolloutManager` that models a ReplicaSet with old and new Pods, applies `maxSurge`/`maxUnavailable` to step through a rolling update, records revision history, performs an undo, and then demonstrates the migration trap where the database schema has moved forward even after the image rolls back. We use the `Account` model with Rajesh and Priya and log each step.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the rollout simulation
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/rollout/*.java
java -cp out com.bank.rollout.RolloutDemo

# Real cluster: update, watch, inspect history, and roll back
kubectl set image deployment/transfer-service transfer=nbi/transfer-service:v6
kubectl rollout status deployment/transfer-service          # waits for rollout
kubectl rollout history deployment/transfer-service          # list revisions
kubectl rollout undo deployment/transfer-service --to-revision=5
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a 4-replica Deployment at v5, upgraded to v6 with a database migration, then rolled back.

Step 1 — The Deployment starts with 4 ready Pods running v5. The revision history records v5.

Step 2 — We deploy v6 with `maxSurge: 1` and `maxUnavailable: 0`. The manager adds one v6 Pod, waits for its readiness, then retires one v5 Pod. It repeats four times, so at no moment are fewer than 4 Pods serving. After the loop all Pods run v6 and the history records v6.

Step 3 — The v6 migration runs and adds a NOT NULL `fee_currency` column to the trades table. A transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya runs fine under v6 because v6 code populates the new column.

Step 4 — We discover a fee bug in v6 and run `rollout undo`. The manager pops v6 from history, scales the v5 ReplicaSet back up, and all Pods run v5 again. The current image is v5.

Step 5 — v5 code tries to insert a trade but does not set `fee_currency`. The column still exists because the migration was never reverted, so the insert violates the NOT NULL constraint and fails. The log raises the rollback-trap warning, proving that rollback restored the image but not the schema.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A rolling update is the default way Kubernetes replaces Pods, and it is controlled by two knobs. The surge setting is how many Pods it may temporarily run above the desired count, and the unavailable setting is how many of the desired Pods may be missing at once. For a banking payment service I set surge to one and unavailable to zero, which means Kubernetes adds one new Pod, waits for its readiness probe to pass, and only then retires one old Pod, so the serving capacity never dips below the target and no customer transfer is dropped during the deploy.

Rolling back is fast because Kubernetes keeps a history of the previous ReplicaSets. Running rollout undo simply scales the chosen old ReplicaSet back up and the current one down, which is itself another rolling operation that respects the same surge and unavailability rules. I can roll back to the immediately previous revision or target a specific revision number from the rollout history.

The subtlety that separates a junior from a senior answer is understanding what rollback does not do. A Deployment revision only snapshots the Pod template, meaning the image, environment variables, and resource settings. It does not capture external state. If a release shipped a new ConfigMap value, a new Secret, or a forward database migration, then rolling back the image leaves all of that external state at its new value. In my project at the National Bank of India this bit us once: a release added a non-null column to the trades table, and when we rolled the image back, the older code did not populate that column and every insert failed the not-null constraint.

The lesson I carry from that is to make deployments rollback-safe by construction. Database changes follow an expand-then-contract pattern so both the old and new code can run against the same schema, which means a rollback is always safe. Configuration is shipped as a new immutable ConfigMap per release and referenced from the Pod template, so a template rollback automatically points back at the matching old config. With those two disciplines in place, rollout undo becomes a genuine safety net rather than a trap that makes an incident worse.
